docs.title: Pathogen Genomic Intelligence Framework — Dashboard Guide
docs.text:
Pathogen genomic data can provide valuable insights into emerging health threats, outbreak dynamics, and the evolution of infectious diseases. When interpreted alongside epidemiological and public health information, these data can help public health professionals understand outbreak patterns, identify changes in circulating pathogens, and inform decisions about surveillance and response.

The Pathogen Genomic Intelligence Framework (PGIF) translates pathogen genomic findings into accessible, public health-oriented intelligence. This guide supports public health professionals, epidemiologists, and outbreak response teams in exploring the dashboard, understanding its visualizations, interpreting findings in their epidemiological context, and recognizing their implications for public health action.

Each section provides a practical guide to the results presented in the dashboard, explaining what the findings may indicate, what conclusions can reasonably be drawn, the limitations of the available evidence, and what additional information may be needed to support public health decisions. Throughout, findings are labelled by the strength of evidence behind them — observed, estimated, or model-derived — and the dashboard deliberately avoids forecasting where the underlying data is too sparse to support it.

How this guide is organized

Each dashboard page gets one chapter, written step-by-step with screenshots from a real pipeline run. Where a number or plot comes from, the chapter says so — the dashboard only shows what the analysis computed; it never invents results. Technical terms are explained where they appear, and the genomic results glossary covers the rest.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• New to PGIF? → Getting started (install → run the analysis → open the dashboard).
  • Already have results? → Jump to Navigation & species selection, then follow the Dashboard guide in order, or open the chapter matching the panel you are looking at.
  • Looking at a finding you don't trust? → Interpreting results and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: The dashboard at a glance
docs.text: Dashboard page Question it answers Intelligence Overview What did the analysis find, and how confident should we be? Biological Threat Have we seen this pathogen before — and how close is it to known references? Pathogen Genomics Where does it sit among known viruses, and which mutations distinguish it? Transmission & Spread How did this lineage spread historically, and how intense was transmission? Geographic & Temporal Context Where and when was it — and its relatives — circulating? Countermeasure Readiness Do vaccines, therapeutics, or diagnostics exist — and how strong is the evidence? Evidence & Knowledge Gaps What does the literature say — and what do we still not know? Intelligence Brief The shareable written summary for decision-makers.

docs.title: Pipeline documentation
docs.text:
Technical reference for the underlying analysis pipeline:

  • Usage — how to run the pipeline, inputs, and parameters
  • Output — every file the pipeline produces
  • Contributing — development guidelines

docs.title: pgirl/genomic-intelligence: Contributing guidelines
docs.text:
Hi there! Thanks for taking an interest in improving pgirl/genomic-intelligence.

This page describes the recommended nf-core way to contribute to both pgirl/genomic-intelligence and nf-core pipelines in general, including:

  • General contribution guidelines: common procedures or guides across all nf-core pipelines.
  • Pipeline-specific contribution guidelines: procedures or guides specific to the development conventions of pgirl/genomic-intelligence.

docs.title: Contribution quick start
docs.text:
To contribute code to any nf-core pipeline:

  • [ ] Ensure you have Nextflow, nf-core tools, and nf-test installed. See the nf-core/tools repository for instructions.
  • [ ] Check whether a GitHub issue about your idea already exists. If an issue does not exist, create one so that others are aware you are working on it.
  • [ ] Fork the pgirl/genomic-intelligence repository to your GitHub account.
  • [ ] Create a branch on your forked repository and make your changes following pipeline conventions (if applicable).
  • [ ] To fix major bugs, name your branch patch and follow the patch release process.
  • [ ] Update relevant documentation within the docs/ folder, use nf-core/tools to update nextflow_schema.json, and update CITATIONS.md.
  • [ ] Run and/or update tests. See Testing for more information.
  • [ ] Lint your code with nf-core/tools.
  • [ ] Submit a pull request (PR) against the dev branch and request a review.

If you are not used to this workflow with Git, see the GitHub documentation or Git resources for more information.

docs.title: GitHub Codespaces
docs.text:
You can contribute to pgirl/genomic-intelligence without installing a local development environment on your machine by using GitHub Codespaces.

GitHub Codespaces is an online developer environment that runs in your browser, complete with VS Code and a terminal. Most nf-core repositories include a devcontainer configuration, which creates a GitHub Codespaces environment specifically for Nextflow development. The environment includes pre-installed nf-core tools, Nextflow, and a few other helpful utilities via a Docker container.

To get started, open the repository in Codespaces.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Once you have made your changes, run the pipeline with nf-test to test them locally. For additional information, use the --verbose flag to view the Nextflow console log output.

nf-test test --tag test --profile +docker --verbose

If you have added new functionality, ensure you update the test assertions in the .nf.test files in the tests/ directory. Update the snapshots with the following command:

nf-test test --tag test --profile +docker --verbose --update-snapshots

When you create a pull request with changes, GitHub Actions will run automatic tests. Pull requests are typically reviewed when these tests are passing.

Two types of tests are typically run:

docs.title: Lint tests
docs.text:
nf-core has a set of guidelines which all pipelines must follow. To enforce these, run linting with nf-core/tools:

nf-core pipelines lint <pipeline_directory>

If you encounter failures or warnings, follow the linked documentation printed to screen. For more information about linting tests, see nf-core/tools API documentation.

docs.title: Pipeline tests
docs.text: Each nf-core pipeline should be set up with a minimal set of test data. GitHub Actions runs the pipeline on this data to ensure it runs through and exits successfully. If there are any failures then the automated tests fail. These tests are run with the latest available version of Nextflow and the minimum required version specified in the pipeline code.

docs.title: Patch release
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Only in the unlikely event of a release that contains a critical bug.

  • [ ] Create a new branch patch on your fork based on upstream/main or upstream/master.
  • [ ] Fix the bug and use nf-core/tools to bump the version to the next semantic version, for example, 1.2.3 → 1.2.4.
  • [ ] Open a Pull Request from patch directly to main/master with the changes.

docs.title: Pipeline contribution conventions
docs.text: nf-core semi-standardises how you write code and other contributions to make the pgirl/genomic-intelligence code and processing logic more understandable for new contributors and to ensure quality.

docs.title: Add a new pipeline step
docs.text:
To contribute a new step to the pipeline, follow the general nf-core coding procedure. Please also refer to the pipeline-specific contribution guidelines:

  • [ ] Define the corresponding input channel into your new process from the expected previous process channel.
  • [ ] Install a module with nf-core/tools, or write a local module (see default processes resource requirements), and add it to the target <workflow>.nf.
  • [ ] Define the output channel if needed. Mix the version output channel into ch_versions and relevant files into ch_multiqc.
  • [ ] Add new or updated parameters to nextflow.config with a default value.
  • [ ] Add new or updated parameters and relevant help text to nextflow_schema.json with nf-core/tools.
  • [ ] Add validation for relevant parameters to the pipeline utilisation section of utils_nfcore_\_pipeline/main.nf subworkflow.
  • [ ] Perform local tests to validate that the new code works as expected.
  • [ ] If applicable, add a new test in the tests directory.
  • [ ] Update usage.md, output.md, and citation.md as appropriate.
  • [ ] Lint the code with nf-core/tools.
  • [ ] Update any diagrams or pipeline images as necessary.
  • [ ] Update MultiQC config assets/multiqc_config.yml so relevant suffixes, file name cleanup, and module plots are in the appropriate order.
  • [ ] If applicable, create a MultiQC module.
  • [ ] Add a description of the output files and, if relevant, images from the MultiQC report to docs/output.md.

To update the minimum required Nextflow version, see the Nextflow version bumping section below. For more information about pipeline contributions, see pipeline-specific contribution guidelines.

docs.title: Channel naming schemes
docs.text:
Use the following naming schemes for channels to make the channel flow easier to understand:

  • Initial process channel: ch_output_from_<process>
  • Intermediate and terminal channels: ch_<previousprocess>_for_<nextprocess>

docs.title: Default parameter values
docs.text:
Parameters should be initialised and defined with default values within the params scope in nextflow.config. They should also be documented in the pipeline JSON schema.

To update nextflow_schema.json, run:

nf-core pipelines schema build

The schema builder interface that loads in your browser should automatically update the defaults in the parameter documentation.

docs.title: Default processes resource requirements
docs.text:
If you write a local module, specify a default set of resource requirements for the process.

Sensible defaults for process resource requirements (CPUs, memory, time) should be defined in conf/base.config. Specify these with generic withLabel: selectors, so they can be shared across multiple processes and steps of the pipeline.

nf-core provides a set of standard labels that you should follow where possible, as seen in the nf-core pipeline template. These labels define resource defaults for single-core processes, modules that require a GPU, and different levels of multi-core configurations with increasing memory requirements.

Values assigned within these labels can be dynamically passed to a tool using the the ${task.cpus} and ${task.memory} Nextflow variables in the script: block of a module (see an example in the modules repository).

docs.title: Nextflow version bumping
docs.text:
If you use a new feature from core Nextflow, bump the minimum required Nextflow version in the pipeline with:

nf-core pipelines bump-version --nextflow . <min_nf_version>

docs.title: Images and figures guidelines
docs.text: If you update images or graphics, follow the nf-core style guidelines.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This document describes the output produced by the pipeline. Most of the plots are taken from the MultiQC report, which summarises results at the end of the pipeline.

The directories listed below will be created in the results directory after the pipeline has finished. All paths are relative to the top-level results directory.

docs.title: Pipeline overview
docs.text:
The pipeline is built using Nextflow and processes data using the following steps:

  • Nextclade - Pathogen classification and clade assignment
  • Nextstrain - Phylogenetic tree building
  • Annotations - Tip metadata and mutation matrix extraction
  • Figures - Annotated phylogenetic tree visualisations
  • MultiQC - Aggregate report
  • Pipeline information - Report metrics generated during the workflow execution

docs.title: Nextclade
docs.text:
Output files
  • nextclade/results/
  • *.tsv: Nextclade classification results per sample.
  • *.json: Detailed JSON output with clade assignments and mutations.
  • *.aligned.fasta: Reference-aligned sequences.

Nextclade assigns sequences to clades, calls mutations, and performs quality checks against a reference dataset.

docs.title: Nextstrain
docs.text:
Output files
  • nextstrain_ebola/
  • results/<species>/all-outbreaks/tree.nwk: Phylogenetic tree in Newick format.
  • results/<species>/all-outbreaks/muts.json: Per-node mutation data.
  • results/<species>/all-outbreaks/branch_lengths.json: Branch length data.
  • auspice/*.json: Auspice JSON for interactive visualisation.

The Nextstrain/augur pipeline builds a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree, infers ancestral states, and exports results for interactive visualisation in Auspice.

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text:
Output files
  • nextstrain_ebola/annotations/
  • <species>_tip_metadata.tsv: Tip-level metadata (country, clade, QC, mutations).
  • <species>_mutation_matrix.tsv: Binary matrix of top 5 amino-acid mutations per protein.
  • <species>_mutation_legend.tsv: Legend mapping mutation columns to genes and frequencies.
  • <species>_node_metadata.tsv: Internal node metadata.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
Output files
  • nextstrain_ebola/figures/
  • <species>_ggtreeExtra.png: Annotated rectangular phylogeny with branches colored by country and a binary heatmap of top amino-acid mutations.

Tree figures are generated with ggtree and ggtreeExtra. Query tips are highlighted with red diamonds.

docs.title: MultiQC
docs.text:
Output files
  • multiqc/
  • multiqc_report.html: a standalone HTML file that can be viewed in your web browser.
  • multiqc_data/: directory containing parsed statistics from the different tools used in the pipeline.
  • multiqc_plots/: directory containing static images from the report in various formats.

MultiQC is a visualization tool that generates a single HTML report summarising all samples in your project. Most of the pipeline QC results are visualised in the report and further statistics are available in the report data directory.

Results generated by MultiQC collate pipeline QC from supported tools e.g. FastQC. The pipeline has special steps which also allow the software versions to be reported in the MultiQC output for future traceability. For more information about how to use MultiQC reports, see http://multiqc.info.

docs.title: Pipeline information
docs.text:
Output files
  • pipeline_info/
  • Reports generated by Nextflow: execution_report.html, execution_timeline.html, execution_trace.txt and pipeline_dag.mmd (raw Mermaid DAG).
  • pipeline_metro_map_*.html — auto-generated nf-metro metro-map diagram of the run's task graph, converted from pipeline_dag.mmd (skipped with a warning if nf-metro is unavailable).
  • Reports generated by the pipeline: pipeline_report.html, pipeline_report.txt and software_versions.yml. The pipeline_report* files will only be present if the --email / --email_on_fail parameter's are used when running the pipeline.
  • Reformatted samplesheet files used as input to the pipeline: samplesheet.valid.csv.
  • Parameters used by the pipeline run: params.json.

Nextflow provides excellent functionality for generating various reports relevant to the running and execution of the pipeline. This will allow you to troubleshoot errors with the running of the pipeline, and also provide you with other information such as launch commands, run times and resource usage.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Panels that look wrong almost always trace to one of a handful of causes. Check these first.

docs.title: "No species found" on every page
docs.text: The app can't see <outdir>/pathogen_identification/. Fix the Pipeline --outdir field in the sidebar, or run the pipeline. Details: Launching the dashboard.

docs.title: Narrative notes look generic ("template" source)
docs.text:
The LLM wasn't reachable when GENERATE_TREE_NOTES / GENERATE_SPREAD_ASSESSMENT / GENERATE_INTELLIGENCE_BRIEF ran — the pipeline writes a deterministic template instead of skipping the section.

  • Fix: make sure Ollama is installed with a pulled model, then run through ./bin/run_with_ollama.sh (it starts/stops the server for you).
  • Verify locally: ollama list and curl http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags.

docs.title: Transmission & Spread: "How did it behave historically?" is empty
docs.text:
The section needs background genomes with a resolvable strain (clade → lineage → outbreak), a date, and coordinates. Symptom-to-cause map:

  • No strains at all → background tips have no clade in the warehouse. Influenza JSONs store clade under clade_membership (seasonal) or label_clade (avian), not clade — fixed in load_background_from_auspice; rebuild the warehouse.
  • Timeline collapses to one month → tip dates were missing. Auspice stores dates as num_date (decimal year), not date — the loader now converts both; rebuild.
  • Map draws nothing / spread stats blank → background samples had no sample_geo_location link or coordinates. Now populated from database/country_centroids.csv at load; rebuild.

After any of these fixes, -resume re-runs BUILD_KNOWLEDGE_DB and COMPUTE_TRANSMISSION_CONTEXT and the section fills in.

docs.title: Mutation landscape is flat (all entropy ≈ 0)
docs.text: The landscape needs translated protein FASTAs (results/<build>/translations/*.fasta) to compute per-position amino-acid entropy. The seasonal-flu build produces them; some avian builds currently don't, so the plot falls back to mutation counts with entropy = 0. The underlying mutation tables are still correct — only the landscape plot is starved.

docs.title: Geographic map is empty or the slider spans one month
docs.text: Same root cause as the historical section — background genomes need dates + coordinates (see above). The slider is built from min(date) → max(date); a collapsed slider means only the query had a date.

docs.title: A panel says "No transmission data for this species"
docs.text: Check whether results/transmission_context/<species>/strain_transmission_profile.tsv exists and has rows beyond its header. A header-only TSV means the upstream warehouse query found no qualifying background genomes — usually missing strain/date/coordinate data.

docs.title: R or Python dependency errors at launch
docs.text: The dashboard auto-installs missing CRAN/Bioconductor packages on first run but needs an internet connection to do it. For air-gapped use, pre-create the pgirl_dashboard conda env.

docs.title: pgirl/genomic-intelligence: Usage
docs.text: Documentation of pipeline parameters is generated automatically from the pipeline schema and can no longer be found in markdown files.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This pipeline performs multi-pathogen genomic epidemic intelligence analysis. It accepts consensus FASTA sequences and sample metadata, classifies them using Nextclade, builds phylogenetic trees via the Nextstrain framework, and produces annotated tree visualisations.

docs.title: Samplesheet input
docs.text:
You will need to create a samplesheet with information about the samples you would like to analyse before running the pipeline. Use this parameter to specify its location. It has to be a comma-separated file with 3 columns, and a header row as shown below.

--input '[path to samplesheet file]'

docs.title: Samplesheet format
docs.text:
Each row represents one set of consensus sequences and associated metadata for a pathogen species:

samplesheet.csv
sample,fasta,metadata
ebola_bdbv,input/bdbv_sequences.fasta,input/bdbv_metadata.tsv
ebola_sudv,input/sudv_sequences.fasta,input/sudv_metadata.tsv
Column Description sample Unique sample/species identifier. Spaces are automatically converted to underscores (_). fasta Full path to consensus FASTA file (.fasta, .fa, .fna, optionally gzipped). metadata Full path to metadata TSV/CSV file (must contain at minimum: strain, date, country columns).

An example samplesheet (assets/samplesheet.csv) can be provided with the pipeline.

docs.title: Running the pipeline
docs.text:
The typical command for running the pipeline is as follows:

nextflow run pgirl/genomic-intelligence \
    --input ./samplesheet.csv \
    --outdir ./results \
    --pathogen ebola \
    --species bdbv,sudv \
    -profile conda

This will launch the pipeline with the docker configuration profile. See below for more information about profiles.

Note that the pipeline will create the following files in your working directory:

work                # Directory containing the nextflow working files
<OUTDIR>            # Finished results in specified location (defined with --outdir)
.nextflow_log       # Log file from Nextflow
# Other nextflow hidden files, eg. history of pipeline runs and old logs.

If you wish to repeatedly use the same parameters for multiple runs, rather than specifying each flag in the command, you can specify these in a params file.

Pipeline settings can be provided in a yaml or json file via -params-file <file>.

[!WARNING] Do not use -c <file> to specify parameters as this will result in errors. Custom config files specified with -c must only be used for tuning process resource specifications, other infrastructural tweaks (such as output directories), or module arguments (args).

The above pipeline run specified with a params file in yaml format:

nextflow run pgirl/genomic-intelligence -profile docker -params-file params.yaml

with:

params.yaml
input: './samplesheet.csv'
outdir: './results/'
pathogen: 'ebola'
species: 'bdbv,sudv'
query_samples: 'SAMPLE-0001,SAMPLE-0002'

You can also generate such YAML/JSON files via nf-core/launch.

docs.title: Updating the pipeline
docs.text:
When you run the above command, Nextflow automatically pulls the pipeline code from GitHub and stores it as a cached version. When running the pipeline after this, it will always use the cached version if available - even if the pipeline has been updated since. To make sure that you're running the latest version of the pipeline, make sure that you regularly update the cached version of the pipeline:

nextflow pull pgirl/genomic-intelligence

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
It is a good idea to specify the pipeline version when running the pipeline on your data. This ensures that a specific version of the pipeline code and software are used when you run your pipeline. If you keep using the same tag, you'll be running the same version of the pipeline, even if there have been changes to the code since.

First, go to the pgirl/genomic-intelligence releases page and find the latest pipeline version - numeric only (eg. 1.3.1). Then specify this when running the pipeline with -r (one hyphen) - eg. -r 1.3.1. Of course, you can switch to another version by changing the number after the -r flag.

This version number will be logged in reports when you run the pipeline, so that you'll know what you used when you look back in the future. For example, at the bottom of the MultiQC reports.

To further assist in reproducibility, you can use share and reuse parameter files to repeat pipeline runs with the same settings without having to write out a command with every single parameter.

[!TIP] If you wish to share such profile (such as upload as supplementary material for academic publications), make sure to NOT include cluster specific paths to files, nor institutional specific profiles.

docs.title: Core Nextflow arguments
docs.text: [!NOTE] These options are part of Nextflow and use a single hyphen (pipeline parameters use a double-hyphen)

docs.title: -profile
docs.text:
Use this parameter to choose a configuration profile. Profiles can give configuration presets for different compute environments.

Several generic profiles are bundled with the pipeline which instruct the pipeline to use software packaged using different methods (Docker, Singularity, Podman, Shifter, Charliecloud, Apptainer, Conda) - see below.

[!IMPORTANT] We highly recommend the use of Docker or Singularity containers for full pipeline reproducibility, however when this is not possible, Conda is also supported.

The pipeline also dynamically loads configurations from https://github.com/nf-core/configs when it runs, making multiple config profiles for various institutional clusters available at run time. For more information and to check if your system is supported, please see the nf-core/configs documentation.

Note that multiple profiles can be loaded, for example: -profile test,docker - the order of arguments is important! They are loaded in sequence, so later profiles can overwrite earlier profiles.

If -profile is not specified, the pipeline will run locally and expect all software to be installed and available on the PATH. This is not recommended, since it can lead to different results on different machines dependent on the computer environment.

  • test
  • A profile with a complete configuration for automated testing
  • Includes links to test data so needs no other parameters
  • docker
  • A generic configuration profile to be used with Docker
  • singularity
  • A generic configuration profile to be used with Singularity
  • podman
  • A generic configuration profile to be used with Podman
  • shifter
  • A generic configuration profile to be used with Shifter
  • charliecloud
  • A generic configuration profile to be used with Charliecloud
  • apptainer
  • A generic configuration profile to be used with Apptainer
  • wave
  • A generic configuration profile to enable Wave containers. Use together with one of the above (requires Nextflow 24.03.0-edge or later).
  • conda
  • A generic configuration profile to be used with Conda. Please only use Conda as a last resort i.e. when it's not possible to run the pipeline with Docker, Singularity, Podman, Shifter, Charliecloud, or Apptainer.

docs.title: -resume
docs.text:
Specify this when restarting a pipeline. Nextflow will use cached results from any pipeline steps where the inputs are the same, continuing from where it got to previously. For input to be considered the same, not only the names must be identical but the files' contents as well. For more info about this parameter, see this blog post.

You can also supply a run name to resume a specific run: -resume [run-name]. Use the nextflow log command to show previous run names.

docs.title: -c
docs.text: Specify the path to a specific config file (this is a core Nextflow command). See the nf-core website documentation for more information.

docs.title: Resource requests
docs.text:
Whilst the default requirements set within the pipeline will hopefully work for most people and with most input data, you may find that you want to customise the compute resources that the pipeline requests. Each step in the pipeline has a default set of requirements for number of CPUs, memory and time. For most of the pipeline steps, if the job exits with any of the error codes specified here it will automatically be resubmitted with higher resources request (2 x original, then 3 x original). If it still fails after the third attempt then the pipeline execution is stopped.

To change the resource requests, please see the max resources and customise process resources section of the nf-core website.

docs.title: Custom Containers
docs.text:
In some cases, you may wish to change the container or conda environment used by a pipeline steps for a particular tool. By default, nf-core pipelines use containers and software from the biocontainers or bioconda projects. However, in some cases the pipeline specified version maybe out of date.

To use a different container from the default container or conda environment specified in a pipeline, please see the updating tool versions section of the nf-core website.

docs.title: Custom Tool Arguments
docs.text:
A pipeline might not always support every possible argument or option of a particular tool used in pipeline. Fortunately, nf-core pipelines provide some freedom to users to insert additional parameters that the pipeline does not include by default.

To learn how to provide additional arguments to a particular tool of the pipeline, please see the customising tool arguments section of the nf-core website.

docs.title: nf-core/configs
docs.text:
In most cases, you will only need to create a custom config as a one-off but if you and others within your organisation are likely to be running nf-core pipelines regularly and need to use the same settings regularly it may be a good idea to request that your custom config file is uploaded to the nf-core/configs git repository. Before you do this please can you test that the config file works with your pipeline of choice using the -c parameter. You can then create a pull request to the nf-core/configs repository with the addition of your config file, associated documentation file (see examples in nf-core/configs/docs), and amending nfcore_custom.config to include your custom profile.

See the main Nextflow documentation for more information about creating your own configuration files.

If you have any questions or issues please send us a message on Slack on the #configs channel.

docs.title: Running in the background
docs.text:
Nextflow handles job submissions and supervises the running jobs. The Nextflow process must run until the pipeline is finished.

The Nextflow -bg flag launches Nextflow in the background, detached from your terminal so that the workflow does not stop if you log out of your session. The logs are saved to a file.

Alternatively, you can use screen / tmux or similar tool to create a detached session which you can log back into at a later time. Some HPC setups also allow you to run nextflow within a cluster job submitted your job scheduler (from where it submits more jobs).

docs.title: Nextflow memory requirements
docs.text:
In some cases, the Nextflow Java virtual machines can start to request a large amount of memory. We recommend adding the following line to your environment to limit this (typically in ~/.bashrc or ~./bash_profile):

NXF_OPTS='-Xms1g -Xmx4g'

docs.title: Biological Threat
docs.text:
Have we seen this virus before — and how confident is the identification?

This page compares your submitted genomes against known references. Pick up to five samples and it builds a side-by-side profile: how completely each genome was sequenced, how closely it matches its nearest known relative, and how far it sits from its assigned family group.

docs.title: Step 1 — Pick samples to compare
docs.text:
The bar at the top lists every sample the pipeline confirmed for this pathogen.

  • Type or click to add samples — up to 5 keeps the charts readable.
  • The badge counts your selection; Reset selection clears it.
  • Nothing appears until you pick at least one sample — everything on this page is a comparison view.

In the example below, six Sample0003 segment records are selected (the badge reads "6 samples selected" — segmented genomes appear as one record per segment, so a single isolate can occupy several slots).

docs.title: Step 2 — Read the summary strip
docs.text:
Once samples are selected, three cards summarize the group — in the example: pathogen H3N2, 6 of 9 samples compared, closest outbreak N/A (no confident outbreak match for these genomes):

  • Pathogen — the species all selected samples were identified as.
  • Samples compared — your selection out of the total confirmed.
  • Closest outbreak(s) — the past outbreak(s) these genomes resemble most closely, or N/A.

Where it comes from

The pipeline's identification results (identification_summary.tsv). "Closest" here means closest in genetic similarity — the genomes look alike — not proof of an epidemiological link to that outbreak.

docs.title: Step 3 — Compare the genomic metrics
docs.text:
With two or more samples selected, a grouped bar chart compares six identification metrics — one coloured bar per sample, grouped by metric. The example shows all of it together: the picker (top), the summary strip, and the chart:

Metric What it means Direction Coverage (%) How much of the genome was successfully sequenced Higher is better % Identity to closest reference How similar the genome is to its nearest known match Higher is better Genetic distance to closest reference How many mutations separate it from that match Lower is better QC overall score The classifier's overall quality flag for the sequence Lower is better Distance to assigned clade How far it sits from the centre of its assigned family group Lower is better MSA Identity (%) How similar the query is to the rest of the alignment, on average Higher is better

A taller bar is not always better

The six metrics live on different scales, so each bar is drawn as a percentage of the highest value in its section. Read each group against its direction label: a query standing out on a lower-is-better metric (genetic distance, clade distance, QC score) is the anomaly worth attention — it suggests a novel or unusual genome, or a quality problem.

docs.title: Step 4 — The identification results table
docs.text:
Below the charts, the full table lists every confirmed sample: coverage, QC score, the closest reference genome (with where and when it was collected), % identity, genetic and clade distances, overall alignment similarity, and closest matching outbreak.

  • The checkbox column is synced with the picker — ticking rows here is the same as selecting samples at the top.
  • Sort and filter any column; "Not Provided" in the location field means the reference record simply didn't carry one.

Only confirmed identifications appear

The table is restricted to samples that passed the identification quality check. Rejected samples aren't missing — they're in the last card on this page.

docs.title: Step 5 — Genomic variation profile (radar)
docs.text:
The next card has its own picker and draws a radar chart of how each selected genome differs from the reference: counts of substitutions, deletions, insertions, frameshifts, missing bases, ambiguous characters, and amino-acid changes — with the raw counts in the table below:

  • Each arm is one kind of variation; each coloured shape is one sample.
  • Use it to compare how genomes differ, not just how much: two samples can have identical identification stats but very different profiles — for example, one dominated by genuine substitutions versus another dominated by missing data (a sequencing-quality difference, not a biological one).
  • The table below covers all query samples, not only confirmed ones.

docs.title: Step 6 — Unresolved samples
docs.text:
The last card (collapsed by default) lists samples the classifier could not assign with confidence — ambiguous or rejected calls, with their coverage and QC status.

Treat this as a data-quality queue: poor sequencing or mixed samples explain most rejections, and they're candidates for re-sequencing rather than signals of something new.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
Three reads matter most on this page:

  1. The assignment and outbreak match — does the genome map onto a known threat we already understand?
  2. Coverage and QC — can you trust the call? Low coverage degrades every distance metric; read novelty cautiously on poorly sequenced samples.
  3. The distance columns — a well-sequenced genome sitting far from every reference is a possible novel lineage and a candidate for confirmatory work.

Limitations

  • "Closest outbreak" is genetic similarity, not epidemiological linkage — an old isolate can match a new query purely by relatedness.
  • Identification is against a reference set: a genuinely novel pathogen far from all references may appear as unresolved rather than as a new finding.
  • This page says what the genome is, not what it will do — spread and impact are covered by the Transmission and Geographic pages.

docs.title: Countermeasure Readiness
docs.text:
Do vaccines, therapeutics, diagnostics, or policies exist for this pathogen — and how strong is the evidence behind each?

This page searches the pipeline's screened literature for countermeasure evidence and summarizes it per domain. Two dropdowns drive everything: Species and Countermeasure type.

docs.title: The four countermeasure domains
docs.text: Domain What it summarizes diagnostic Test performance — sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, limit of detection per named test vaccine_therapeutic Product efficacy/effectiveness per named vaccine or drug intervention Non-pharmaceutical intervention effectiveness & coverage (narrative) policy Policy/guidance evidence (narrative + policy table)

docs.title: Reading the current state — an honest empty panel
docs.text:
The screenshot shows the real state of this run: "No countermeasure data — No literature evidence is available for this species."

Empty means 'not computed', not 'none exist'

This message means the literature screening step produced no extracted claims for this species+domain — usually because the literature- evidence extraction wasn't run or yielded nothing, not that H3N2 has no diagnostics or vaccines (it plainly does). Treat an empty page as a data gap to flag, never as a negative finding. The same applies to the 0/11 evidence-coverage figure on the Intelligence Overview.

docs.title: What the page looks like once evidence exists
docs.text:
When screened literature is available for a species, the page fills in top to bottom:

  1. Coverage strip — a one-line count: "X of Y screened papers yielded claims" for the selected domain, plus the overall total. This is the first honesty check — thin denominators mean thin conclusions.
  2. Narrative summary (for intervention and policy) — a generated plain-text summary of the evidence, labelled with its source (ollama/template) the same way as elsewhere.
  3. Metric selector + forest plot (for diagnostic, vaccine_therapeutic) — pick a metric (e.g. sensitivity, efficacy) and see each study's estimate with its confidence interval plus the pooled estimate across studies — the literature's combined answer.
  4. Product / policy table — the per-product or per-policy rows behind the plot: name, metric values, study design, phase, endpoints, and the other context fields extracted from each paper.

How to use the forest plot

  • Points are individual studies; the diamond/pooled row is the combined estimate.
  • Wide intervals = few or noisy studies; a pooled estimate sitting on 2–3 papers is a weak foundation for decisions.
  • Consistent estimates across studies carry more weight than one strong outlier.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
1. Coverage denominators first — "3 of 40 papers yielded claims" is a different world from "30 of 40".
  2. Established countermeasures vs your query's biology — cross-check with the phenotype markers (e.g. an M2:S31N hit makes amantadine evidence irrelevant for that genome).
  3. Narrative summaries are starting points — click through to the underlying table rows before quoting numbers.

Limitations

  • Evidence comes only from the screened literature set — what the pipeline retrieved and extracted, not the world's literature.
  • Pooled estimates inherit the biases of included studies (design, phase, setting).
  • An empty domain is a gap to close, not a finding to report.

docs.title: Evidence & Knowledge Gaps
docs.text:
Section in progress

This page will cover the domain coverage charts (field completeness per evidence domain, papers screened vs claims yielded), the evidence table, the meta-analysis panel, and the species coverage strip.

docs.title: What this page answers
docs.text: What does the published evidence say about this pathogen — and which questions are still unanswered?

docs.title: Geographic & Temporal Context
docs.text:
Where and when was this lineage — and its relatives — circulating?

This page is the genomic-epidemiological reconstruction: it replays the lineage's history on a map — where genomes appeared, how they spread, and which outbreaks they coincided with. Press play on the timeline, or drag it to any date, and everything on the page rebuilds to that moment.

docs.title: Step 1 — The reconstruction view
docs.text:
• Timeline slider (top) — from the lineage's first record (1978-01) to the latest (2026-06). Press play to animate history; drag to pause at a date — the Reconstruction date (Jun 2026) shows where you are.
  • The map — each point is a sampled genome (size roughly by count at that location); the red marker is the query in Uganda. Two overlays can be toggled:
    • Transmission network — edges linking genetically related genomes: inferred links combining genetic divergence + geography + time, with the line pointing toward the newer genome.
    • Spread paths — the reconstructed movement routes between locations.
  • Right panel — the query + closest historical genomes subtree, so the map and the family tree stay side by side.

Inferred edges are hypotheses, not contact tracing

A dashed line from China to Uganda says "these two genomes are close relatives in space-time" — it does not prove the virus travelled that route; unsampled intermediates are common, and the legend below grades how strong each link actually is.

docs.title: Step 2 — Cases, deaths, and the cumulative toll
docs.text:
• Monthly cases/deaths timeline — the epi curve behind the map; the dashed line marks the reconstruction date. Only the period up to your slider position counts.
  • Cumulative donut — the running total at that date: here 242,382 cases, CFR 0% — severity context for the whole lineage at a glance.

  • Link confidence legend — the graded honesty scale for every edge on the map, strongest to weakest:

    Label Meaning CONFIRMED same strain + same country + recent INFERRED same strain or co-located PROBABLE broader geo/genetic proximity CONTEXTUAL epidemiological record only OBSERVED a directly sampled genome

    When a link looks important, check its grade before citing it — CONTEXTUAL is background colour, not evidence of a route.

  • AI geographic note — the local LLM's reading of the reconstruction (here: 3C.2a1b.1a/1b sub-strains emerging in Kenya in 2021/2022, the 1a.1 strain originating in China, and Sample0003's closest matches in China and Kenya while its strain characteristics point to the USA). It ends with the correct caveat itself: links suggest possible routes — they do not definitively prove movement between countries.

  • Chronological event log (below) — the same history as a dated list, for readers who prefer text to the animation.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
1. The reconstruction at the query's sampling date — scrub to it and see which relatives were circulating nearby at that moment.
  2. CONFIRMED/INFERRED edges into the query's country — the plausible importation routes worth follow-up.
  3. Convergence of independent signals — when the tree, the map links, and the epi curve all point the same direction, the story is strong; when only the network edges do, it isn't.

Limitations

  • The map shows sampled genomes — undersampled countries are invisible, which can invent "gaps" and reroute inferred paths.
  • Country centroids are used for locations; an edge connects countries, not cities or individuals.
  • Cumulative counts reflect reported cases — under-reporting understates them.
  • The AI note summarizes the same data you can see; treat its geographic phrasing as suggestive, always checking the link- confidence grade.

docs.title: Influenza Analysis
docs.text:
Do the eight segments tell a coherent story — or a reassortant, defective, or phenotypically interesting one?

This page only exists for influenza (H3N2, H5NX) — influenza's genome comes in eight separate segments that reassort with each other, so it needs checks Ebola doesn't. It answers three influenza-specific questions:

  1. Where did each segment come from? — genotype constellation & reassortment
  2. Does it carry known drug-resistance or virulence markers? — phenotype markers
  3. Are any segments broken? — genome integrity / DI screen

The example below is the H5NX run.

docs.title: Step 1 — Genomic constellation & reassortment
docs.text:
Each segment is typed against its own reference set, then the eight labels are laid side-by-side — the "genotype constellation":

  • Headline counts — isolates screened, how many look like reassortants, and how many carry a novel constellation (a segment combination not seen in the background set).
  • The coloured strip — one row per isolate, one column per segment (pb2 → ns). Each cell is that segment's genotype/lineage label. A row of the same colour family = a coherent genotype; a row mixing labels from different subtype families = a mosaic.
  • Reassortment flags table — per isolate, true/false and why: e.g. "ns typed as h3n2 … np typed as h1n1pdm … pa typed as h1n1pdm (isolate species h5nx)" — segments whose typing disagrees with the isolate's declared species, or labels that differ from the group's modal constellation.

How to read a reassortant flag

Reassortment is normal influenza biology — a flag means "these segments have different histories", not "this is dangerous". It becomes important when a marker (Step 2) or a novel constellation comes along with it.

docs.title: Step 2 — Phenotype markers
docs.text:
The pipeline checks the query against a curated catalogue of mutations with published associations — antiviral resistance, virulence, and host adaptation:

Read across each row:

  • mutation / category / phenotype — e.g. M2:S31N → antiviral_resistance → "Amantadine/rimantadine resistance — most common M2 marker (>99% of circulating seasonal A)".
  • drug — which countermeasure the association affects, where relevant (amantadine, oseltamivir, peramivir).
  • confidence — established (well-replicated literature) vs suspected (reported but weaker).
  • coordinate_caveat — the honesty column: e.g. "within +/-1 of N1-numbered position — verify subtype numbering" or "marker characterized in h5n1, this run is h5nx". Numbering differs between subtypes, so a hit may need manual confirmation.
  • source — the catalogue entry it came from (who_m2_page, who_nai_table, cdc_h5n1_inventory, …).

Associations, not verdicts

The page footer says it plainly: these are phenotype associations from a curated catalogue — not clinical calls. M2:S31N tells you amantadine almost certainly won't work; NA:D199N says "suspected" reduced oseltamivir inhibition — worth flagging to the lab for phenotypic testing, not enough alone to change treatment guidance. Rows with a coordinate caveat always need a human check first.

docs.title: Step 3 — Genome integrity (DI / truncation screen)
docs.text:
A defective-interfering (DI) or truncated segment is a sequencing or biological red flag — this screen scans each record's Nextclade QC for signs of one:

  • Headline counts — records screened, flagged, isolates affected.
  • Coverage tiles — one column per segment, one row per record; colour = coverage, red border = DI/truncation flag. In the example both isolates have a pale/red untyped cell at ~0–9% — a segment that essentially failed to assemble.
  • Flag table — the evidence per flagged record: coverage, deletion count, frameshifts, premature stops, failed CDS translations, and the full reason string (e.g. large_deletion_count=46; frameshifts=4; premature_stop_codons=3; failed_cds=N,P_V_C,M,L; low_coverage=0.06_with_deletions).

What a flag means — and doesn't

  • Most flags are assembly/sequencing problems: a segment that failed to assemble is missing data, not necessarily a biologically defective particle. Check before interpreting it biologically.
  • A flag also weakens every other panel for that segment — its tree placement, typing, and mutation calls are unreliable, and this is often why a segment shows as untyped in the constellation.
  • True DI confirmation needs read-level coverage — this is a consensus-level screen, as the page itself states.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
1. Reassortant + marker together — a novel constellation carrying a resistance/virulence marker is the combination that escalates interest.
  2. Established-confidence resistance markers — M2:S31N-type hits feed directly into the Countermeasure Readiness page.
  3. Flagged segments — treat every downstream claim about that segment as provisional until re-sequenced.

Limitations

  • Constellation labels depend on the typing reference set — an unusual label can mean "novel" or "unrepresented in the background".
  • Marker hits transfer between subtypes imperfectly (see the coordinate-caveat column).
  • The DI screen is consensus-level and conservative — it errs toward flagging poor assemblies.

docs.title: Intelligence Brief
docs.text:
Section in progress

This page will cover the full-page generated brief: the situation summary, per-query transmission assessments, the evidence digest, and the export flow (Preview & Edit → download Markdown / print to PDF).

docs.title: What this page answers
docs.text: What is the shareable, written summary a decision-maker can read in two minutes?

docs.title: Intelligence Overview (home)
docs.text:
The Intelligence Overview is the landing page for the selected pathogen — a one-screen summary designed for a quick read: what did the analysis find, how much confidence does it deserve, and where do I look next?

This walkthrough uses an influenza run (H3N2) as the example:

Reading top to bottom, the page carries four things: the assessment badges (the verdict), the situation strip (what was submitted), the narrative (a written summary), and the evidence cards (one per analytical layer, each a doorway into a full page). The card header itself — Intelligence Brief — h3n2 plus the family badge — is also the species dropdown, kept in sync with the navbar switcher described in Navigation & species selection.

docs.title: Step 1 — Read the assessment badges
docs.text:
At the top of the card, a row of badges compresses the whole analysis into a verdict. In the screenshot above they read MONITOR · Confidence: High · Transmission risk: low · Narrative: ollama, followed by the generation timestamp:

  • Assessment — MONITOR, INVESTIGATE, or ESCALATE: how unusual the genome looks compared with everything we already know about. It is a cautious, transparent rule set — not a model making predictions — and it only escalates on novelty signals (the genome sitting unusually far from its closest known relative or its assigned family group), and only when the underlying data is good enough to trust.
  • Confidence — High / Medium / Low / Insufficient evidence: how solid the underlying data is, driven mainly by how much of each genome was successfully sequenced (coverage). Low confidence never pushes the assessment toward ESCALATE — it simply means "don't over-read this."
  • Transmission risk — short labels summarizing what the transmission analysis found for each query genome (e.g. sustained human transmission).
  • Narrative source — whether the paragraph below was drafted by the local AI assistant (ollama) or assembled from a fixed template (template). See Troubleshooting if you expected AI text.

Two separate axes

Assessment answers "how worrying is this genome?"; Confidence answers "how good is the data behind that call?" A clean, ordinary genome on solid data reads MONITOR · High confidence; a possibly-novel genome on thin data reads INVESTIGATE · Medium confidence. The rules almost never reach ESCALATE from identification evidence alone — that is deliberate.

docs.title: Step 2 — Scan the situation strip
docs.text:
Four headline numbers summarize what was submitted — in the example above: 9 query genomes, 2 countries (Uganda + an unknown location), collection dates Jan 30–31, 2026, median coverage 98.9%:

  • Query genomes — how many submitted samples were identified as this pathogen.
  • Countries — where those samples were collected; Unknown appears when a sample's metadata didn't carry a location.
  • Collection dates — earliest to latest sampling date.
  • Median coverage — how completely the genomes were sequenced, on average; the main input to the Confidence badge.

docs.title: Step 3 — Read the narrative
docs.text:
The blue-bordered paragraph is the generated situation summary: a plain-language synthesis of what the analysis found across identification, genomics, transmission, and the published evidence. In the example it ties the nine H3N2 genomes to their closest known reference (A/Washington/106/2016), reports the estimated R at sampling, and flags that the geographic link between the Ugandan samples and the matched U.S. transmission cluster is unclear — exactly the kind of caveat a reader should carry forward.

Where it comes from

Written during the analysis run and stored in intelligence_brief.json. When the local AI assistant is available it writes the paragraph; otherwise a fixed template fills in the same facts. Either way, every number in it traces back to a result table — it never contains a figure you can't find elsewhere in the dashboard.

docs.title: Step 4 — Walk the four evidence cards
docs.text:
Below the narrative, four clickable cards summarize each layer of evidence — clicking one jumps straight to the full page for that question.

What is it — identification. The closest known reference genome and how similar the query is to it, plus the closest matching past outbreak — in the example, H3N2 identified with 97.6% identity to A/Washington/106/2016 and a small genetic distance, i.e. a close match to a known, previously circulating strain. Click → Biological Threat.

What's different about it — genomics. Whether the query carries more mutations than its background relatives (with a statistical significance check), which mutations are linked to known traits, and which proteins most distinguish it — plus two mini-plots:

  • Divergence boxplot — how far each query sits from the root of the family tree (red dots) compared with the background distribution. A query far above the box is unusually divergent.
  • Top proteins — the proteins whose mutations most separate the query from background genomes.

Click → Pathogen Genomics.

How it's spreading — transmission evidence. Whether the queries belong to known genetic clusters, where the lineage most likely originated, how many separate introductions the data suggests, and the estimated R at sampling — the average number of people each case infected at the time the samples were taken — plus a mini-map of where the query's relatives were collected.

In the example below: 1 genetic cluster, likely origin USA, China; Kenya, R at sampling 3.48, and the map's dashed line connecting a U.S.-sampled relative to the Ugandan query — a visual hint of possible importation that the narrative also flags as uncertain.

What we know & what we can do — evidence & countermeasures. How much published research yielded usable findings, how many evidence areas are covered, and the leading countermeasure product — plus an AI/auto highlights summary and two small charts.

Here the card is deliberately honest about having nothing: 0/11 domains with evidence, no papers with claims, and a note that the evidence-summary step didn't run. Empty does not mean reassuring — it means the literature-evidence layer hasn't been computed for this species yet.

Click → Evidence & Knowledge Gaps.

docs.title: Step 5 — Check the caveats
docs.text: The amber Caveats strip (visible at the bottom of the screenshot) lists the analysis' own warnings — here three important ones: 1 of 9 genomes failed identification QC (so the species call is provisional), no phenotype-linked mutation evidence, and no literature-evidence counts for this species. Read it before quoting any number further — it is the dashboard telling you exactly how far to trust what you just saw.

docs.title: Step 6 — The objectives strip
docs.text: Beneath the cards, a muted row of tiles mirrors the sidebar's objective list — a reminder of what else is available without competing with the assessment above.

docs.title: Public-health relevance
docs.text:
This page is built for the 60-second read: a duty officer should be able to say "the analysis found H3N2, confidence is high, transmission evidence is moderate, here is the summary" — and know exactly which card to click for the supporting evidence. Everything shown is observed or estimated from data; the verdict is a transparent rule set, not a black box.

Limitations

  • The assessment currently uses identification signals only; it is first-pass triage, not a full risk assessment.
  • "Insufficient evidence" means missing data, not low threat.
  • AI-drafted and template narratives differ in phrasing, not in facts.

docs.title: Navigation & species selection
docs.text: How the dashboard is organized and how to move between pathogens. Every other chapter assumes you can do the three things on this page.

docs.title: The landing screen: pathogen cards
docs.text:
When the app loads, the home page is a pathogen-family selector — one card per family the run detected, so you only ever see dashboards for pathogens that were actually found in your genomes.

Each card shows:

  • the family name and a one-line summary of its biology (for example, a segmented genome means the dashboard will offer per-segment views);
  • the species detected in your run as badges — here BDBV, EBOV, SUDV under Ebola and H3N2, H5NX under Influenza;
  • an "Open … dashboard" button that takes you into that family's Intelligence Overview.

Why families, not just a species list

Different pathogens need different views — a segmented influenza genome gets per-segment analyses that a single-genome filovirus doesn't. You pick the family first; the dashboard then shows only what applies to that biology.

The button row also includes a reset — the "change pathogen" flow returns you to these cards at any time.

docs.title: The global pathogen switcher
docs.text:
Once a family is selected, a dropdown is pinned to the centre of the top navbar, next to a family badge:

  • It lists every detected species grouped by family, so you can jump between, say, SUDV and H3N2 without going back to the cards.
  • The pill-shaped badge beside it names the family of the current species.
  • It stays visible on every tab — the current pathogen is never ambiguous.

docs.title: The sidebar
docs.text:
The sidebar is organized around the eight intelligence objectives. Sections expand per species, and only objectives with real data get full pages — the rest show a short "Planned" roadmap note.

Sidebar group Contains Intelligence Overview The assessment-first home page for the selected species INTELLIGENCE OBJECTIVES Biological Threat → per-species pages; Pathogen Genomics → Phylotree and Mutation submenus INFLUENZA ANALYSIS (influenza runs only) Segment-signatures pages Objectives continued Transmission & Spread, Geographic & Temporal Context, Countermeasure Readiness — one page per species EVIDENCE & REPORTING Evidence & Knowledge Gaps, Intelligence Brief

Tip

Expanding one objective auto-collapses the others — only one tree stays open at a time, so the sidebar never scrolls far.

docs.title: The --outdir field
docs.text: Top of the sidebar: the Pipeline --outdir text box. Change it and the whole app reloads against a different results directory — useful for comparing two runs. See Launching the dashboard.

docs.title: How pages relate
docs.text:
Most visualizations deep-link into each other:

  • Clicking a section card on the Intelligence Overview jumps straight to the corresponding objective page (e.g. "What's different about it" → Pathogen Genomics).
  • The Pathogen Genomics landing page offers per-species Phylotree and Mutation shortcuts.
  • The Intelligence Brief aggregates facts from every section into one exportable document.

The flow mirrors an analyst's read: what is it → what's different → how is it spreading → where/when → what can we do → what's the brief.

docs.title: Pathogen Genomics
docs.text:
Where does this virus sit on the family tree — and which mutations set it apart?

Pathogen Genomics has two sub-pages in the sidebar:

  • Phylotree — the phylogenetic tree: how your genomes relate to known background viruses.
  • Mutation — the mutation profile: which changes distinguish your genomes and whether any of them matter.

Both work the same way for every pathogen; for influenza, a segment selector additionally lets you look at each of the eight genome segments separately.

docs.title: Step 1 — Choose what to show on the tree
docs.text:
The Annotation Layers panel (left) toggles what each tip displays:

  • Clade coloring — tips coloured by their family group (the clade names appear in the legend).
  • Outbreak labels — mark tips belonging to known named outbreaks.
  • Country / Genome coverage / Mutation count — colour tips by where they were collected, how complete the sequence is, or how many mutations they carry.
  • Query highlight — marks your submitted genomes so they stand out against the background.

The tree itself can be drawn Rectangular or Circular, with Fit tree to view and the spacing/zoom sliders to adjust readability.

How to read the tree

Tips are genomes; branch length is genetic distance — how many mutations separate them. Your query sitting on a short branch inside a well-known clade means "looks familiar"; a query on a long branch away from everything means "unusual" — worth a closer look, not a verdict.

docs.title: Step 2 — Switch genome segments (influenza)
docs.text:
For segmented viruses, the Segment dropdown swaps the whole tree — each segment has its own evolutionary history:

This matters because a query can look typical on HA but unusual on NP — an early hint of reassortment (segments with different histories being inherited together). Comparing where the query sits across segments is one of the most informative quick reads for influenza.

docs.title: Step 3 — Read the AI tree note
docs.text:
Above the tree, a short paragraph summarizes the placement — in the example it notes that Sample0003 from Uganda clusters with U.S. background genomes of the 3C.2a1 clade sampled in 2016, and cautions that the geographic link can't be resolved from the data alone.

  • The AI badge (qwen2.5:14B) means it was written by the local LLM; template would mean a fixed-rule summary instead.
  • Regenerate asks the LLM for a fresh wording of the same facts.
  • The note is a reading aid — every claim in it traces to the tree data underneath. When it says "uncertain", that's the honest answer, not a hedge.

Below the tree, a Tip Details table lists the same information per genome (clade, country, date, divergence) for precise lookup.

docs.title: Step 4 — The overview: PLS-DA score plot
docs.text:
The PLS-DA score plot compresses all mutation differences into two axes — points that cluster together carry similar mutation profiles:

  • Colour samples by — country, outbreak, or collection_year (shown: a year gradient, older samples dark, recent bright).
  • Click any point to see what it is — the tooltip shows the sample name, group (Background/Query), year, country, outbreak, and mutation burden.
  • Find a sample (right) — jump straight to a named genome.
  • The AI Mutation landscape note on top summarizes what the plot means for this run.

What to look for

If your query points sit inside the background cloud, its mutations look typical. A query drifting away on PC1 or PC2 carries an unusual combination of changes — the next steps tell you which ones.

A MANOVA table beneath the plot tests formally whether the query group differs from background.

docs.title: Step 5 — Per-protein mutation positions
docs.text:
The next panel asks which proteins carry unusual mutations?

  • Each x-axis position is a protein; the grey violins show the spread of mutation counts across all background genomes; the red dot is your selected query.
  • p < 0.001 labels flag proteins where the query's count is unusual.
  • Pick a different query in the right-hand selector — its per-protein positions and z-scores update in the table beside it.
  • The Y-axis metric/scale and Sort x-axis controls re-arrange the view.

A query dot above its violin — e.g. on HA — means that protein carries more substituted positions than background relatives usually do.

docs.title: Step 6 — The mutation landscape
docs.text:
The Mutation Landscape zooms down to single amino-acid positions: for every position in the selected protein, how variable it is across all background genomes (Shannon entropy — tall peak = the position changes a lot across strains):

  • Segment / protein dropdowns choose which protein to show (HA1 shown).
  • Red dots mark positions where your query differs from the reference — read them against the background entropy: a red dot on a tall peak is a mutation at a commonly-varying position (likely tolerated); a red dot on a flat, conserved position is more interesting — backgrounds almost never change there.
  • Checkboxes restrict the view to query positions or phenotype-annotated positions; the position box jumps to a residue.
  • Hover any point for the details: reference residue, entropy, how many background/query genomes are mutated there.

docs.title: Step 7 — One mutation in depth
docs.text:
Clicking a position opens the detail card — everything the pipeline knows about that substitution:

  • Substitution chips (top) — every amino acid seen at that position, with its share of query and background genomes (N→K at 100% of the query, 97.9% of background).
  • Temporal trend — when that variant rose in circulation (here, the K variant swept in around 2017 — a historical fixation, not a new event).
  • Geographic map — where genomes carrying it were sampled.
  • Sequence logo — which residues dominate that position overall.
  • Amino-acid property change — whether the swap changes the chemistry: here Asparagine (polar, neutral) → Lysine (basic, positive), flagged Non-conservative substitution — the kind worth a virologist's attention even though it's common in background.
  • Where the pipeline's annotation data covers it, the card also reports documented phenotype/biological significance (resistance, virulence, host adaptation).

How to weigh a mutation

High background prevalence + an old temporal rise = established variant, probably tolerated by the virus. Rare/absent in background + non-conservative chemistry + a phenotype annotation = the mutations genuinely worth flagging.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
1. Tree placement — inside a known clade (familiar) vs a long isolated branch (worth scrutiny).
  2. Per-segment disagreement (flu) — different stories on different segments suggest reassortment.
  3. Query-specific mutations on conserved positions — especially non-conservative ones with documented phenotypes.

Limitations

  • The tree shows sampled history — unsampled transmission is invisible.
  • PLS-DA and MANOVA describe association, not causation.
  • Landscape entropy needs translated protein files; segments lacking translations can show a flat line (see Troubleshooting).
  • The AI note is a summary aid — the numbers in the tables are the ground truth.

docs.title: Transmission & Spread
docs.text:
How did this lineage spread historically, how intense was transmission where the query sits, and is the query part of an ongoing cluster?

This page reads like a short report in six labelled sections — A through F — moving from the query's place on the tree to a final assessment statement. Every number in it is either observed history or a fitted estimate on observed data; nothing projects the future.

No forecasts by design

Earlier versions projected future cases. That was removed: the pipeline doesn't collect enough covariates to project responsibly, so this page reports observed history and fitted estimates only.

docs.title: The header — pick a genome, get its dossier
docs.text:
Choose the query in the dropdown — everything below updates. The strip then answers "what do we already know about this genome?":

  • Strain / Clade / Lineage / Outbreak — its family placement (3C.2a1, no named outbreak here).
  • Location — where it was collected (Uganda).
  • Likely origin — the background country its closest relatives point to (USA) — a phylogenetic hint, not travel-history proof.
  • R at sampling — transmission intensity where/when it was collected (R≈3.48; section C shows the uncertainty around it).
  • Cluster = cases — what fraction of the cluster's genomes map to reported cases (17.3%) — a rough genomics-to-epidemiology bridge.

docs.title: A. Genomic relationship & how it spread — observed history
docs.text:
The tree shows the query (red star) among its closest sampled relatives; below it, the lineage's movement summary:

  • Spread rate — 1971.1 km/yr: how fast this lineage moved geographically across its sampled history.
  • Max extent / Countries / Origin — 15126 km span, 3 countries, origin Australia (where the deepest sampled ancestor sits).

Read 'origin' cautiously

Origin and spread rate are computed from sampled genomes — they describe where the sequenced record starts, which can lag or miss the true source country entirely.

docs.title: B. Closest relatives — outbreak impact over time — observed history
docs.text:
For the countries where the query's closest relatives circulated, the panels show monthly reported cases (left) and monthly deaths (right) — the real-world footprint of the lineage your genome belongs to.

In the H3N2 example, cases show clear seasonal peaks through 2016–2026 while deaths stay essentially flat — a high-circulation, low-severity profile typical of seasonal influenza rather than, say, an Ebola signature. This is the epidemiological counterpart to the genetic tree.

docs.title: C. Transmission intensity — estimated R(t)
docs.text:
The R(t) curve plots the time-varying reproduction number in the query's location, with the dashed line marking when the query was sampled:

  • At sampling, R = 3.48 (95% CrI 0.70–8.38) — the credible interval is the honest part: with sparse data it spans "under control" to "growing fast", so the dashboard concludes stable or uncertain rather than pretending precision.
  • Shaded band = 95% credible interval; spikes earlier in the series are past transmission surges at that location.

R(t) is a location estimate, not a genome property

R(t) describes transmission in that place at that time, estimated from reported cases — it isn't a property of this virus specifically, and wide intervals mean "we can't tell", not "we can't be bothered".

docs.title: D. Genetic transmission cluster — tree-derived
docs.text:
The orange callout says it directly:

Query is genetically distinct — no background genome falls within the transmission-cluster threshold, so it likely represents a separate introduction or an unsampled lineage.

"Cluster = cases" in the header and this section are the same idea at different scales: does the query sit inside a sampled transmission cluster? Here the answer is no — which usually means either a separate introduction or, very commonly, that the actual cluster simply wasn't sequenced.

docs.title: E. How did it behave historically? — observed history
docs.text:
Compare the query's strain (and optionally others) on its track record:

  • 3C.2a1: 306.75 linked cases, 0 linked deaths, 0% mean CFR, 3 countries, 4 years active, behaviour = persistent, multi-country.

This is the strain's resume — the counterfactual question it answers is "what has this lineage done before?", which is the strongest observed evidence for what it might do again.

docs.title: F. Transmission & Spread Assessment
docs.text:
The final card writes the conclusions in two clearly-labelled voices:

  • OBSERVED — what the historical record shows: "linked to 306 cases across three countries … persisted for four years without recorded deaths … likely originated in the USA based on its genetic characteristics."
  • MODEL-DERIVED — what the fitted estimates add: "R ≈ 3.48 with a wide range of 0.7–8.4 … growth phase stable or uncertain … slow doubling time of about 38 days … sparse weekly cases, so reliability may be limited."

The footer states the rule the whole pipeline follows: Observed = historical evidence. Model-derived = growth-model fit to observed data. The AI-generated tag (qwen2.5:14b) marks the prose; the numbers are the pipeline's.

Limitations

  • R(t) and spread rate inherit every gap in case reporting and sequencing density — wide credible intervals are the norm in sparse settings.
  • Origin / likely origin describe the sampled record; undersampled regions routinely misattribute it.
  • "Genetically distinct" ≠ "new lineage" — it most often means the real cluster wasn't sequenced.
  • The assessment card is a summary; the numbers in sections A–E are the evidence to cite.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
1. R(t) with a credible interval clearly above 1 at sampling — this example is ambiguous, a sustained R > 1 with tight bounds is not.
  2. Query inside a defined cluster with a short branch to a named outbreak — the closest thing to "ongoing transmission" genomics can show.
  3. A strain resume that disagrees with the badge — e.g. MONITOR next to a lineage with documented high-CFR history would deserve a second look.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Two environments are involved: the pipeline environment (Nextflow + conda, runs the analyses) and the dashboard environment (R + Shiny, displays the results). You need the pipeline env to produce results, and the dashboard env to view them.

docs.title: 1. Pipeline environment
docs.text:
conda create -n nf-genomic-intelligence nextflow conda
conda activate nf-genomic-intelligence

The pipeline itself pulls its per-process dependencies via the -profile conda flag — Nextflow creates the process environments on first run, so the first execution is slower than subsequent ones.

docs.title: 2. Dashboard environment
docs.text:
The dashboard needs its own R environment (pgirl_dashboard):

conda env create -f envs/pgirl_dashboard.yml
conda activate pgirl_dashboard

First launch auto-installs missing packages

If a package is missing, app.R installs it from CRAN / Bioconductor on first launch (shiny, bs4Dash, DT, plotly, leaflet, duckdb, ggtree, treeio, ...). That first start can take a few minutes; later launches are fast.

docs.title: 3. Optional: local LLM summaries
docs.text:
Some panels show AI-written narrative notes (tree notes, spread assessment, intelligence brief). These are generated locally by Ollama — no data leaves your machine.

# macOS
brew install ollama
ollama pull qwen2.5:14b     # default model configured in nextflow.config

The pipeline default is qwen2.5:14b at http://127.0.0.1:11434 (see params.ollama_host / params.ollama_model in nextflow.config). Run the pipeline through bin/run_with_ollama.sh and Ollama is started/stopped for you. If Ollama is unavailable, the pipeline still writes every narrative — just as a deterministic template note instead of an LLM note (the dashboard marks which is which).

docs.title: What gets installed where
docs.text: Component Where it runs Environment Nextflow pipeline your machine or HPC nf-genomic-intelligence Shiny dashboard your machine, in a browser pgirl_dashboard Ollama (optional) your machine (localhost:11434) system install This docs site GitHub Pages (edit locally with mkdocs serve) any Python ≥3.9

docs.title: Launching the dashboard
docs.text: The dashboard is a standalone Shiny app — it is not part of the Nextflow run. Run the pipeline first, then launch the app whenever you want to browse results.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
From the repository root:

conda activate pgirl_dashboard
Rscript -e "shiny::runApp('dashboard')"

This starts a local web server and opens your browser (typically http://127.0.0.1:port). Leave the terminal running — closing it ends the session. In RStudio you can also open dashboard/app.R and click Run App.

docs.title: Point it at your results
docs.text:
The only thing the app needs to know is where your --outdir is.

  1. In the sidebar, find the Pipeline --outdir field at the top.

  2. It defaults to results (i.e. ../results relative to dashboard/). Type a different path if your run went elsewhere — absolute paths, ~/…, and repo-root-relative names all work.

  3. The whole dashboard refreshes against that directory.

What 'no species found' means

If every page says No species found, the app can't see <outdir>/pathogen_identification/. Either the pipeline hasn't run yet, or --outdir points somewhere else — check the field first.

docs.title: Pick a pathogen
docs.text:
When results are found, the landing page shows one card per detected pathogen family — so you choose the group of viruses you want to look at before diving into species-level detail.

In this example run you would pick between the two:

  • Ebola — opens views for its detected species (BDBV, EBOV, SUDV): the biological-threat tables, the family tree, the mutation landscape, and transmission context.
  • Influenza — opens views for its species (H3N2, H5NX): everything Ebola gets, plus per-segment analyses because influenza carries eight genome segments — genotype constellations, reassortment flags, segment integrity and group diversity.

Click "Open … dashboard" on a card to enter that family's Intelligence Overview. From then on:

  • The navbar switcher (top centre) shows the current species and lets you switch to any other detected one at any time.
  • The sidebar shows the full menu for that family's species.

docs.title: Light & dark mode
docs.text: The dark-mode toggle (moon/sun icon in the navbar) is supported throughout; all charts and tables have dark variants. Screenshots in this guide use light mode for print readability.

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text: Ctrl+C in the terminal (or stop the R session). Nothing is persisted — the app is read-only against your results/ directory.

docs.title: Running the pipeline
docs.text: Everything the dashboard shows comes out of one Nextflow run. This page walks through the command used for the worked example in this guide (an Ebola / influenza mixed FASTA with metadata), then the options that matter most for the visualizations.

docs.title: The example run
docs.text:
./bin/run_with_ollama.sh main.nf -profile conda \
  --fasta input/all/all_fasta.fasta \
  --metadata input/all/all_metadata.tsv \
  --outdir ./results \
  --epi_min_year 2015 --epi_max_year 2026 \
  --skip_literature true --skip_iqtree true \
  -resume

Step by step:

  1. ./bin/run_with_ollama.sh main.nf ... — the wrapper starts a local Ollama server (if one isn't already running), polls until it answers, runs Nextflow with the remaining arguments, then stops only the server it started. Without it, LLM narrative notes fall back to template text.
  2. -profile conda — per-process conda environments are created automatically.
  3. --fasta / --metadata — the query genomes and their sample metadata. The pipeline classifies every sequence (Nextclade), groups them by detected species, and runs the per-species branches (Ebola via nextstrain-ebola, seasonal flu via pgirl builds, avian flu via segment-focused builds).
  4. --outdir ./results — all dashboard data lives under here. Keep it stable; the dashboard points at this directory.
  5. --epi_min_year 2015 --epi_max_year 2026 — the epidemiological window. !!! warning "Don't anchor this to your query's year" The historical-comparison panels only work when background genomes from earlier years are in scope.
